title: Many Gifts, One Body
overview: Paul tells a proud, divided church that its varied spiritual abilities all come from one God and exist to serve everyone, just as the many parts of a body work together.

parts.label: A simple test (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Most of these readers once worshiped idols, where trances and oracles were common, so a powerful experience alone proved nothing. Paul's test is what a speaker says about Jesus: God's Spirit never curses him, and sincerely calling him Lord is itself a sign of the Spirit at work.

parts.label: Different gifts, one giver (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: Paul lists abilities such as words of wisdom, healing, prophecy (speaking a message from God) and tongues, which some understand as real languages the speaker never learned and others as a prayer-like speech no one understands without an interpreter. What several of these gifts were exactly is debated, but his point is plain: God decides who gets what, and every gift is for the good of all, not for showing off.

parts.label: One body made of many (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: Paul compares the church to a human body: many parts, one living whole that belongs to Christ. Jewish and non-Jewish, slave and free, all joined it the same way, through baptism (the water ritual of joining) and one shared Spirit.

parts.label: Every part belongs (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: Paul pictures a foot sulking because it is not a hand. The playful image makes a serious point: people with less impressive gifts belong just as fully, and a body that was all eye could never hear.

parts.label: No part is unneeded (vv. 21-26)
parts.note: Now the warning turns to the gifted who think they need no one. Just as people give extra care to the body's private or fragile parts, the church should honor those who seem least important, so that everyone shares each other's pain and joy.

parts.label: Roles in the church (vv. 27-31)
parts.note: Paul puts apostles (the first messengers sent out by Jesus), prophets and teachers first, likely because they help others most, and places tongues last, perhaps because the Corinthians prized it too highly. His questions expect the answer no, since nobody has every gift, and the better way he promises turns out to be love, the subject of the next chapter.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ over whether the dramatic gifts listed here, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, still happen today or ended with the first generation of the church.
think: Have you ever been part of a group where you felt like the piece that didn't fit, and what would have made you feel you belonged?
